opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I like to think about robotics data as a pyramid, and real robot data sits at the very top of it.

At the bottom of the pyramid, you have internet-scale data: videos, text, images of humans doing all sorts of things. It's massive, it's diverse, and it gives you a lot of common sense and priors about how the world works. But it doesn't have any action labels. You can watch a million YouTube videos of someone cooking, and you still don't know the motor commands to move a robot arm.

In the middle, you have simulation and synthetic data. This is where I think a lot of the scaling will come from, because in simulation you're no longer bound by real-world time. You can run thousands of environments in parallel, randomize physics and visuals, and increasingly use generative models to create new scenes and even neural simulations. That gives you scale and diversity that you just can't get physically.

And at the top, you have real robot data, usually collected through teleoperation. It's the highest quality, because it's exactly the embodiment, the sensors, and the physics you'll deploy in. But it's also extremely expensive and slow. Humans get tired, robots break, and you fundamentally can't collect more than 24 hours of data per robot per day. Real robot data runs on human fuel, and human fuel doesn't scale the way compute does.

So the role of real robot data isn't to be the bulk of the dataset. It's the grounding signal. It closes the sim-to-real gap, it anchors the model to reality, and it serves as the final fine-tuning and evaluation layer. You need all three tiers working together. If you rely only on real data, you can't scale. If you rely only on sim and internet data, you never quite land in the real world. The art of a good data strategy is figuring out the right mixture, and converting compute into data as much as possible so that the expensive real-world data goes much further.

r001.rationale: The response says real robot data matches the deployed embodiment, sensors, and physics, and that it closes the sim-to-real gap.

r002.rationale: It identifies slow collection and the 24-hours-per-robot-per-day ceiling as limits on real-world data gathering.

r003.rationale: It advocates using all three tiers together, with internet data, simulation, and real robot data providing complementary strengths.

fable-5.1.text:
Real robot data is the most precious part of the whole pyramid, and precisely because it's so precious, you can't build your strategy on it alone. I like to think of it as a data pyramid. At the top you have real robot data, teleoperation data, where a human is physically guiding the robot, and that's the gold standard, because there's no sim-to-real gap at all. It's exactly the distribution you want the robot to act in. But it's also incredibly expensive. You're limited by the number of robots you have, the number of operators, and by physics itself. A day only has twenty-four hours, and you can't run a robot faster than real time. So that data grows linearly at best, and you can't scale it the way the language community scaled web text.

That's why the middle of the pyramid is simulation. In sim you're no longer bounded by wall-clock time. You can run thousands of environments in parallel on a GPU and generate what would be years of experience in a few hours. You can randomize physics, lighting, object placement, and get diversity you'd never afford in the real world. The downside is the gap: simulators are never perfectly faithful, so you need techniques like domain randomization to make sure the policy doesn't overfit to the quirks of the engine.

And then the base of the pyramid is the internet-scale data, human videos, text, everything that teaches the model what the world looks like, how objects behave, how people manipulate things. It's noisy, there are no action labels, but there's an ocean of it, and it gives you the priors.

So the role of real robot data in that picture is twofold. First, it's the anchor. It grounds everything from the lower layers in the actual embodiment, the actual sensors and actuators. You use it to fine-tune and to close the last mile. Second, it's your measuring stick. It's what tells you whether your sim and your video pretraining are actually transferring, or whether you've just built a very good policy for a world that doesn't exist. I'd never want to be in a position of having zero real data. But I'd also never want to be in a position where real data is the only lever, because then your scaling curve is just a function of how many teleop rigs you can afford, and that's not a path to general-purpose robots.

r001.rationale: It calls teleoperation data the gold standard because there is “no sim-to-real gap at all.”

r002.rationale: It says robots cannot run faster than real time and that physical limits constrain data growth.

r003.rationale: It describes a data pyramid combining real robot data, simulation, and internet-scale data, emphasizing their complementary strengths and limits.

astra-6.text:
I think real robot data is essential, but it can’t be the entire strategy. If every bit of learning requires a physical robot to perform an action, you’re constrained by hardware, maintenance, and how quickly you can collect diverse experiences.

So I’d think about a combination of sources. Video can help a model learn about the world and how people interact with objects. Simulation lets you practice at scale, vary environments, and explore failures that would be expensive on hardware. Real robot data grounds that learning in what actually happens when you take an action—the contact, the friction, the consequences that are hard to capture perfectly in simulation.

The key is to make those sources work together. Use real-world failures to identify what’s missing, then collect targeted demonstrations or build simulations around those gaps. Real data is both a training resource and the reality check. Ultimately, success means the robot works in the physical world.

r001.rationale: The response says real robot data grounds learning in physical consequences that simulation may miss, but it does not clearly state that real robot data avoids the sim-to-real gap.

r002.rationale: It says relying on physical robots constrains how quickly diverse experiences can be collected, identifying collection pace as a limit.

r003.rationale: It advocates combining video, simulation, and real robot data, and explains the different strengths each source contributes.

sol-6.1.text:
I think real robot data is essential, but it’s one part of the strategy. You also want to learn from simulation and from the enormous amount of visual information available in videos. Those sources give you breadth; real robot experience grounds that knowledge in what the robot can actually do.

The hard part is contact. Watching someone pick up a cup doesn’t tell you exactly how much force to apply, what friction feels like, or how to recover when the cup slips. You need physical interaction to learn and validate those things.

So I’d think of it as a loop: use simulation and other data to build broad capabilities, test them on real robots, and collect real data where the model fails or is uncertain. Then feed those lessons back into training. The goal isn’t simply to collect the most robot hours. It’s to collect experience that improves generalization.

r001.rationale: It says real robot experience grounds learning in what the robot can do, but does not clearly state that real robot data avoid the sim-to-real gap.

r002.rationale: It does not identify the pace of physical-world operation as a limit on collecting real robot data.

r003.rationale: It recommends combining simulation, video, and real robot experience, explaining that they provide breadth and physical grounding.
